short: A Germanic ambush annihilated three legions and fixed the Rhine as Rome's frontier.
full:
In the autumn of 9 CE, the Cheruscan chieftain Arminius, a Roman-trained auxiliary officer, lured Publius Quinctilius Varus and three legions off the road and into wooded, marshy terrain near modern Kalkriese. Over several days of ambush the column was destroyed almost to a man; Varus fell on his own sword rather than be captured. Roman sources put the loss at around 20,000 dead, including the legions XVII, XVIII and XIX, whose numbers were never used again.

Augustus reportedly would not cut his hair for months afterward and was said to cry out for his legions to be returned. The disaster ended any serious Roman ambition to absorb Germania as a province; punitive campaigns under Germanicus followed, but Tiberius abandoned permanent conquest east of the Rhine. The river became the empire's practical frontier for the rest of its history, one of the few Roman defeats to permanently redraw the map.
